label: explain-bm-science
one_line: We test whether printed two-layer plastic strips can curl with damp air, using a maths limit that a computer has checked.
what: A pine cone scale is two layers stuck together. When the air dries, one layer shrinks more than the other, and the scale bends open. We want to know if a 3D printer can make strips that do the same with ordinary printing plastic. We use a formula from 1925 that says how tightly a two-layer strip can bend. A computer program that accepts only complete proofs has confirmed one limit in that formula. The limit says a strip can never curl tighter than 1.5 times the size mismatch divided by its thickness. We use the limit to rule out bad designs on paper before anything is printed. Real printing plastics swell very little in water, so we also check how fast and how far they could move.
why: Plants move with no motor and no power, and a printed part that did this could be useful. Printing a strip and waiting days to see nothing happen wastes time. A rule that rules out hopeless designs saves that time. The limit is not new, since a 2015 paper had already plotted it. What is new is that a computer has now proved it. We do not know yet if a real printed strip will follow the formula.

wrong_if: Here is the bet, written before looking. We say a printed two-layer strip will never curl tighter than 1.5 times the size mismatch divided by its thickness. If we measure a real strip that curls tighter than that, we are wrong. We also bet that thin layers react faster, by roughly the square of the thickness. If a layer half as thick is not much faster, we are wrong about that part. And if a stiff printed layer on a soft one curls far less than the formula says, the formula is not useful here.
could_go_wrong: The formula is for a thin ribbon, and a wide sheet behaves differently, rolling up about 30 to 50 percent tighter in one direction only.
Water soaks into printed plastic very slowly, so a demonstration could take days instead of minutes.
The formula says nothing about speed, creep (slow sagging) or how well the two layers stay glued.
Printing plastics may swell too little to give a bend you can see.
Two Formlabs documents disagree on how much one resin swells in water, probably because they describe two versions of it.
Heat may bend a strip more than damp air does, which would confuse the test unless we vary both.
We could not read three of the original papers in full, so some of what we say about them is second-hand.
Wheat bristles and the twisting seed pod of the orchid tree sit behind paywalls, so we have no numbers for them.

questions.q: How do you know the limit is true?
questions.a: A proof-checking program accepted it with only the three standard starting rules of mathematics. It also rejected a false version that said 7/5 instead of 3/2. A paper from 2015 had also shown the same limit on a graph.

We have not printed or measured any strip. We could not read some original papers in full. We did not test wide sheets, big swelling, creep or glue between layers. The speed numbers for plastics are our own estimates.
No. The limit was already known from plots. The new part is that a computer has proved it.

questions.q: Do real pine cones reach the limit?
questions.a: Close but not quite. They get to about 82 to 97 percent of it, by our own arithmetic. They are not exactly at it.

questions.q: Why not just use a stiffer partner layer to curl more?
questions.a: The formula says the stiffness ratio drops out once the layers are the best thickness. It is the mismatch and the thickness that set the limit.

questions.q: Does ordinary printing plastic swell much in water?
questions.a: Mostly little. A one-centimetre cube of two Formlabs resins gains about 0.7 percent weight in a day. One other resin sheet gained 8 percent in a day, so it depends on the resin and the test.

questions.q: How fast could a printed strip move?
questions.a: Our model says a layer 0.2 to 0.4 millimetres thick of a stock stiff resin takes about 9 to 38 hours. A layer of 0.8 millimetres or more could take days. These are model results, not measurements.

questions.q: Does the formula match what others measured?
questions.a: It follows the trends. It over-predicts the tightest bend of printed soft humidity strips by about four times.

check_yourself.expect: Three files say ALL CHECKED with no errors and exit 0; the negative control says FAILED with exit 1.

check_yourself.what: Re-run the bending arithmetic: the limit, the 1925 formula match, and the soaking times.
check_yourself.expect: A grid maximum of 1.5000000000000002, and a time constant of 0.7239 for curvature.

check_yourself.what: Re-run the ordinary arithmetic for the pine cone, the uptake in drops, and the thin-layer speed-up.
check_yourself.expect: 0.7 percent turns into 7 milligrams per gram, and the soaking constant 0.848 appears.
A maximum of 1.5 on the grid, and a value of 1.25 for the pine cone in Reyssat and Mahadevan.

check_yourself.what: Open the pine cone paper and read how the two layers work.
check_yourself.expect: A paper titled Hygromorphs: from pine cones to biomimetic bilayers.
